summary:
Our goal was to turn the complex world of space mission design into a playable puzzle. Players choose a Star Observation or Telecommunications mission, pick an orbit, then build their spacecraft slot by slot, balancing mass, power, heat, data and radiation against a strict budget. Every component is based on real hardware and mission data from NASA, ESA and partner agencies, with missions like Kepler, Gaia and TBIRD as references. Pack too little onboard storage and your data is lost before it reaches Earth; skimp on radiation shielding and your electronics fail before the mission ends. Only a design that passes the readiness review gets approval to launch.

We tackled this challenge because systems engineering is usually locked away in dry technical documents. By wrapping hard science in an immersive, nostalgic command-line interface, we made the real math of spaceflight accessible and surprisingly fun. It matters because it shows the public that launching a rocket is only half the battle. The real challenge is the brutal, unforgiving puzzle of keeping the payload alive in the dark.

GitHub link: https://github.com/vaggeliskg/nasa_space_mission
details:
Terrastrum is a retro, 80s-style command-line simulator that puts you in the seat of a mission’s Lead Systems Engineer. You aren’t piloting a spaceship; you are designing the spacecraft itself. Players work through a vintage terminal interface, guided by Commander Vance, our stern NPC. The game loop is simple but unforgiving. You choose a primary directive, either Exoplanet Photometry or a High-Rate Telecom Relay, pick an orbit, then configure your spacecraft slot by slot: bus size, instrument, power, communications, attitude control, propulsion, thermal control, radiation shielding, onboard computer and end-of-life plan.
When your design is locked, the engine checks every choice against real engineering rules and hardware data in a final readiness review. If your thermal system can’t handle the heat load, your electronics overheat. If you don’t pack enough onboard storage, your data is lost before you can downlink it to Earth. If your shielding is too thin, your computer fails before the mission ends. Only a design that passes every check gets approval to launch. It’s a ruthless balance of mass, power and budget against survival.

The main benefit is demystifying the reality of space systems engineering and project management. Most space games focus on launching rockets or dogfighting. We wanted to highlight the unseen heroes: the engineers who must keep a delicate sensor cold and stable while the spacecraft bakes in sunlight and radiation.
Our intended impact is educational. We want players to understand why space missions cost millions, even billions, and take years to plan. By making the math playable, we hope to build public appreciation for the careful engineering that NASA, ESA and their partner agencies do every day.

Team Spacebuds wanted the game to be instantly accessible to judges and the public, so we skipped heavy 3D engines and chose a web stack. The core engine and UI are built with React and Next.js, in TypeScript: strict typing was essential to handle the mathematical constraints and hardware parameters without breaking the game state.
For the visuals, we used CSS with Tailwind to recreate the glowing green phosphor text, CRT scanlines and screen flicker of a 1980s monitor. The project is version-controlled on GitHub and deployed on Vercel, so it runs instantly in any browser

Our biggest creative choice was text over graphics. Instead of a 3D interface, we leaned into the “Cassette Futurism” aesthetic: a glowing terminal creates real tension and nostalgia. It feels like sitting in a 1980s Mission Control room, where every keystroke decides the fate of a multi-million-euro project.
To keep the game authentic, we built the logic from real hardware specifications and mission data, using missions like Kepler, Gaia, ASTERIA and TBIRD as references. Where public data existed, we used it; where it didn’t, we scaled estimates from similar hardware and marked them clearly. The hardest factor was balance: turning heavy concepts like pointing accuracy in arcseconds or shielding thickness in g/cm² into mechanics a gamer can grasp without a physics degree.
dataRefs: NASA Small Spacecraft State of the Art (SOA) Report (Communications & Optics)
